segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say there should be something to eat?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: There should be something to eat. So we said that should was would owe or would must. So what is to owe, which we can use like must, and it's related to debt?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Deber.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Deber. And would must or would owe gives us the meaning should.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Debería.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. There should be something to eat.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Debería haber...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Your first place your mind is going to go is to choose between ser and estar. If neither fit, make that little check. Oh, is this exist? Is this the be that means exist? And then you know it's haber. So there should be, there should exist, something to eat.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Debería haber algo comer...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ...para comer.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. In order to eat. There should be something in order to eat. Good. Debería haber algo para comer. There should be something to eat. Very good. Another common place that we use the mood tense in Spanish is when we say it is an adjective, que, and then a verb. This verb is going to go into the mood tense. You are noticing that que has a lot to do with the subjunctive, that this que introduces the mood tense in many cases. So for example, if I want to give you some advice and tell you it's terrible that you eat this, it is terrible that you eat this. So let's speak informally.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Es terrible que comas esto.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Es terrible que comas esto. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So it's the que, the combination of es terrible and que which introduces this mood tense. If you say it is terrible if you eat this, then you don't use the mood tense. So how would you say that? It is terrible if you eat this, still speaking informally.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Es terrible si comes esto.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Es terrible si comes esto. How would you say it is possible?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Es posible.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. How would you say it's possible that we go later? What is later or more late?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Más tarde.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And what is the root for the mood tense of go? Voy, va becomes...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Vaya.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So it is possible that we go later.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Es posible que vayamos más tarde.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Es posible que vayamos más tarde.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Fuerte in Spanish means strong, but it's also used colloquially, and maybe the closest translation that I can think of would be something like, I mean, again, it's very colloquial, but you could say, "Oh, that's hardcore. That's full on." Ah? In Spanish, you say a lot, "¡Qué fuerte! ¡Qué fuerte!" How heavy, how hardcore, how full on, ¡qué fuerte! And we see that we can use qué like how: ¡Qué fuerte! ¡Qué lindo! How nice, how beautiful. ¡Qué bueno! How good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: You can say ¡qué increíble que...! or ¡qué fuerte que...! So whilst we have two qués there, in Spanish this is just how incredible that, ah? How hardcore that. And of course, we would carry on into the mood tense. So how strong, [CHUCKLE] how heavy that he is here? How would you say that?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Qué fuerte que esté aquí.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. ¡Qué fuerte que esté aquí! In English, we achieve a similar feeling to what we get with the Spanish subjunctive sometimes with words like should or might. Here, for example, in English, we could say how incredible that he should come. Here we don't mean should like in its literal meaning like debería, no? Here in English, we are using should to give this kind of mood tense feeling. How incredible that he should come.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Está bien, está bien means it's okay. The literal translation of bien is well, and to be well is a state, so it goes with estar: está bien. But it can also be used like it's okay. So for example, you could say, you know, it's okay that you ask, but I don't have to reply. So to ask is preguntar,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: and to reply or to respond is responder. So we will say it's okay that you ask, but it's not necessary that I respond. I don't need to respond; it's not necessary that I respond. So the first bit: it's okay that you ask, and we're speaking informally, and to ask was preguntar.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Está bien que preguntes.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Está bien que preguntes. So it's like, okay, you can ask as much as you like, ah? So this is the feeling we get here with the mood tense. Or in English, we might use might here to get this kind of mood tense feeling: it's okay that you might ask. But...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Pero...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ...it's not necessary that I respond. I don't need to respond; it's not necessary that I respond. There's a few ways we can say this.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No es necesito...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Necesito is the verb.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Necesidad? No, is necessity. [LAUGH]

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Is necessity. So necessary, how is vocabulary in Spanish?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Wait. Necesario.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So it's not necessary that I respond.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No es necesario que responda.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. Está bien que preguntes, pero no es necesario que responda. And there we have the mood tense after es necesario or no es necesario que. So we have it is, adjective, que, and then the verb, and that verb with the mood tense. We also could have said no hace falta que responda, it doesn't make lack, this common expression we said that we will hear around: hacer falta. No hace falta que responda.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say it is important that we find it soon? It's important that we find it soon.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Es importante que lo encontremos pronto.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Es importante que lo encontremos pronto. Good.
